title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
description: Understand the critical distinction between functional and non-functional requirements and why both are essential for successful system design.

data.text: Every system design interview begins with requirements, but not all requirements are created equal. Functional requirements describe **what** the system should do, while non-functional requirements define **how well** it should do it. Mastering this distinction is the foundation of effective system design.

Functional requirements are the explicit features and behaviors the system must support. They answer questions like: Can a user upload a video? Does the system send email notifications? Can an admin delete a user account? These requirements are usually black and white — either the feature works, or it does not.

data.title: Common Functional Requirements:
items: Data creation, reading, updating, and deletion (CRUD)

data.text: Non-functional requirements describe the quality attributes of the system. They define constraints on system behavior and often determine whether a design succeeds or fails in production. Non-functional requirements are frequently left unstated in interviews, making it critical to ask targeted questions.

rows: Should the API respond in under 200ms?
How many concurrent users are expected?

data.title: Interview Tip
data.text: Always ask about scale, latency, and availability first. These three non-functional requirements shape the majority of your architecture decisions.

data.caption: Classification of system requirements
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[System Requirements] --> B[Functional]
    A --> C[Non-Functional]
    B --> B1[Features]
    B --> B2[User Actions]
    B --> B3[Business Rules]
    C --> C1[Performance]
    C --> C2[Reliability]
    C --> C3[Scalability]
    C --> C4[Security]

data.text: A system with perfect functional requirements but poor non-functional attributes will fail in the real world. For example, a social media app that lets users post photos but takes 10 seconds to load is unusable. Similarly, a highly scalable system with no useful features serves no purpose. The best designs balance both dimensions from the very first interview question.

terms.definition: A specific behavior or feature the system must provide, such as user login or data export.
A quality attribute describing how the system should perform, such as latency, availability, or scalability.
A non-functional property like performance, security, or maintainability that affects overall system quality.

items.question: Can a requirement be both functional and non-functional?
items.answer: Rarely. Requirements are typically classified as one or the other. However, a feature like 'search' is functional, while 'search results must load in under 100ms' is non-functional.

items.question: Which should I clarify first in an interview?
items.answer: Start with functional requirements to understand the core problem, then immediately pivot to non-functional constraints like scale, latency, and availability.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Functional requirements define what the system does
Non-functional requirements define how well it performs
Always ask about scale, latency, and availability early
Use the classification diagram to organize requirements
data.takeaway: Great system designers clarify both functional and non-functional requirements before drawing a single box on the whiteboard.
